body:
FOUND 2026-08-12 by the T34 lane (PR #401) while building the quarantine envelope, and deliberately left out of that diff because it is an ERASURE gap rather than a budget one. Pre-existing.

WHAT IS WRONG. Containers nest. `drop()` on an INTERMEDIATE container does not reach a pool nested beneath it: that pool's store is orphaned — no longer reachable through the tree, and still on disk. The lane's envelope report now RECURSES the nesting; `drop()` does not. So the two disagree about what the tree contains, and the one that disagrees in the dangerous direction is the one that removes bytes.

WHY THIS IS THE SERIOUS CLASS. §11's promise is not that a purge is attempted, it is that erasure is PROVABLE — the operator can be told the bytes are gone and be right. An orphaned store is bytes at rest that no sweep visits and no report mentions. That is the H7 shape at its worst: not a purge that failed loudly, but a purge that never knew the bytes existed, reporting completeness over a set it had already lost track of. Judge this ticket the way CLAUDE.md says to judge every erasure change: not `does it remove the bytes` but `can this report be false`.

MEASURE FIRST. Build the nesting (primary → intermediate container → pool with its own store), write something into the nested pool, `drop()` the intermediate, and then look AT THE BYTES: is the pool's store still on disk, and does any report mention it? Record what you find. If a sweep already reaches it by some path the lane did not see, say so with the evidence and close this.

MEASURED 2026-08-14 (branch t162-drop-orphan, probe commit 1652baa): confirmed. After `mid.drop()` reported success, a fresh handle on the nested pool's sqlite path still held the secret delta and the file still carried its plaintext marker; a nested store that retained bytes could not force a refusal. Repaired by sharing ONE traversal (`poolsBeneath`, envelope.ts) between the envelope report and drop's discard fan-out.

THE REPAIR, if measurement earns it: the fan-out follows the same recursion the report now uses, so the two cannot drift — one traversal, two consumers. Prefer that over teaching `drop()` its own second walk; two walks that must agree is the defect shape T139, T158 and T160 all turned out to be.

RAILS, and the standing rule is absolute here: EVERY erasure rail is TWO-SIDED. The nested pool's bytes are gone from disk after the drop AND a named live bystander — a sibling container, and the primary itself — still reads and still has its bytes. A rail that only proves removal cannot see over-purging, which on this surface is the unrecoverable direction.

WHO MERGES: MYK, without exception. This WIDENS WHAT GETS PURGED — a store that previously survived a drop would now be removed — and CLAUDE.md reserves that direction for him every time. The PR must state in one line what can now be deleted that could not before.

OVERTAKEN (stale sweep, 2026-08-25): Landed as PR #414 (commit c129eda on main): poolsBeneath in src/gateway/envelope.ts:320 is the shared traversal consumed by both the envelope report and drop's fan-out (container.ts:1354), with rail test/gateway/drop-nested-orphan.test.ts in the tree. The shard was never archived (status in-progress) — archive it with adlc ticket archive T162 --write --authorize, never delete.
title: `drop()` on an intermediate container orphans a nested pool's store — outside the report AND outside §11's fan-out
